title: On the uniqueness of the strictly convex quadrilateral central configuration with a fixed angle

candidates.exact_quote: Lemma 1. For any \(r \in \tilde{\mathcal{C}}\), we have \(\nabla_r F_4(r) = \nabla_r C(r) \cdot A(r)\).
candidates.claim_content: Setting: four points P1,P2,P3,P4 in the plane with mutual distances r_ij, d_ij := r_ij^2. F_4(r) is the 4-point Cayley–Menger determinant, i.e. the determinant of the 5x5 matrix [[0,1,1,1,1],[1,0,d12,d13,d14],[1,d12,0,d23,d24],[1,d13,d23,0,d34],[1,d14,d24,d34,0]], which equals 288 V^2 (V = tetrahedron volume), so F_4 = 0 exactly for planar configurations. For a FIXED constant angle θ one defines C(r) = 2 r12 r34 cos θ + r23^2 + r14^2 − r24^2 − r13^2, and A(r) = 32 V_{124} V_{234} where V_{ijk} is the area of the triangle P_iP_jP_k. The paper claims that at every r with C(r)=0 one has ∇_r F_4(r) = A(r) · ∇_r C(r), i.e. the gradients of F_4 and of C are parallel there. Test configuration (a strictly convex, anticlockwise quadrilateral): P1=(0,0), P2=(2,0), P3=(2.5,1.5), P4=(0.5,2), giving d12=4, d13=8.5, d14=4.25, d23=2.5, d24=6.25, d34=4.25, and cos θ = 8/8.24621 = 0.970143 (so C(r)=0 and F_4(r)=0). At this point A = 32 V_{124}V_{234} ≈ 104.0, and direct computation gives ∂F_4/∂d13 = −A ≈ −104.0 while ∂F_4/∂d12 = (17/16) A ≈ 110.5, whereas ∂C/∂d13 = −1 and ∂C/∂d12 = r34 cos θ / r12 = 1. Hence (∂F_4/∂d12)/(∂F_4/∂d13) = −17/16 ≠ −1 = (∂C/∂d12)/(∂C/∂d13), so ∇F_4 is NOT a multiple of ∇C. (Since d_ij = r_ij^2 the Jacobian of the change of variables is diagonal, so parallelism in d-coordinates is equivalent to parallelism in r-coordinates.)
candidates.suspected_defect: The factorisation F_4 = C·A used to prove Lemma 1 is not valid as an identity of functions of r for a fixed θ: for a fixed θ the surface {C=0} is NOT contained in {F_4=0} (configurations with C=0 can be genuinely 3-dimensional whenever cos θ lies strictly between cos(α+β) and cos(α−β)), so the two hypersurfaces meet transversally and their gradients are not parallel. The numeric test above exhibits a strictly convex planar quadrilateral where the gradient ratios are 17/16 versus 1. Since Proposition 3 (equivalence of critical points of W̃ = U + λ(I−I0) + σF_4 and of W = U + λ(I−I0) + ηC) rests entirely on this parallelism, the whole reduction, and hence Theorem 1, collapses (except in the trapezoid case θ=0, where C=0 does imply planarity).

candidates.exact_quote:
Proposition 2. *For a strictly convex quadrilateral configuration \( r \in \mathcal{G} \),*

\[
(11) \qquad F_4(r) = C(r) \cdot A(r),
\]
candidates.claim_content: With d_ij = r_ij^2, F_4(r) the 4-point Cayley–Menger determinant (determinant of [[0,1,1,1,1],[1,0,d12,d13,d14],[1,d12,0,d23,d24],[1,d13,d23,0,d34],[1,d14,d24,d34,0]]), C(r) = 2 r12 r34 cos θ + d23 + d14 − d24 − d13 with θ a FIXED parameter, and A(r) given by Eq. (14) first line, A(r) = 2( d24(d13 − d34) + d12(d23 − d24 − d34) + d14(−d23 + d34) + 2 r12 d24 r34 cos θ ), the paper asserts F_4(r) = C(r)·A(r). Question: is this an identity in the six distances (for fixed θ)? Note that F_4 does not contain θ at all, while the product C·A contains the term (2 r12 r34 cos θ)(4 r12 d24 r34 cos θ) = 8 d12 d24 d34 cos^2 θ, and no other term of C·A is quadratic in cos θ.
candidates.suspected_defect: F_4 is independent of θ but C·A contains a nonvanishing cos^2 θ term with coefficient 8 d12 d24 d34, so F_4 = C·A cannot hold identically in r for a fixed θ; it can hold only on the subset where C=0 and F_4=0 simultaneously. This invalidates the differentiation performed in Lemma 1 ('From (11) we have ∇F_4 = ∇C·A + C·∇A'), which requires the product form to hold in an open neighbourhood.

candidates.exact_quote: Since we can define that θ = 0 if the line P_{1}P_{2} and P_{3}P_{4} are parallel, i.e., a trapezoid shape, hence θ ∈ [0, π/2]
candidates.claim_content: The paper claims that for every strictly convex quadrilateral P1P2P3P4 (vertices in anticlockwise cyclic order) the angle θ appearing in the constraint C(r) = 2 r12 r34 cos θ + r23^2 + r14^2 − r24^2 − r13^2 = 0 can be taken in [0, π/2] (so cos θ ≥ 0). From the paper's own derivation (Eq. (15)–(17)), cos θ = cos(β − α) where α = ∠P1P2P4 and β = ∠P2P4P3. Counterexample: take P2=(0,0), P4=(1,0), P1=(−0.5, 0.866) (so r12 = 1, α = 120°), P3=(0.436, −0.205) (so r34 = 0.6, β = 20°). All four cross products of consecutive edge vectors are positive, so P1P2P3P4 is a strictly convex anticlockwise quadrilateral. Its distances are r12=1, r24=1, r34=0.6, r14=√3≈1.7321, r23≈0.4818, r13≈1.4224, and C(r)=0 forces 1.2 cos θ + 0.2091 = 0, i.e. cos θ ≈ −0.174, θ ≈ 100° > π/2.
candidates.suspected_defect: cos θ = cos(β−α) can be negative for strictly convex quadrilaterals (θ can be obtuse), so the restriction θ ∈ [0, π/2] is false. This matters because the topology proof (Lemma 3) uses Θ(θ) = 1/cos θ + 1 ≥ 2, which requires cos θ ∈ (0,1]; configurations with obtuse θ are not covered at all.

candidates.error_location: Section 2.2, remark after the definition of \tilde{\mathcal{C}}
candidates.exact_quote: we can easily check that the collinear and the strictly concave configurations are not in this set
candidates.claim_content: The paper defines, for a fixed angle θ, the set \tilde{C} = { r ∈ G : C(r) = 0 } where C(r) = 2 r12 r34 cos θ + r23^2 + r14^2 − r24^2 − r13^2 and G is the set of realizable mutual-distance vectors of four points, and asserts that no strictly concave quadrilateral configuration lies in \tilde{C}. Counterexample with θ = π/2 (cos θ = 0): P1=(0.5,1), P2=(0,0), P3=(0.6,0.2), P4=(1,0). Here P3 lies strictly inside triangle P1P2P4, so the simple quadrilateral P1P2P3P4 is strictly concave (reflex at P3). Its squared distances are r12^2 = 1.25, r13^2 = 0.65, r14^2 = 1.25, r23^2 = 0.40, r24^2 = 1, r34^2 = 0.20, and C(r) = 0 + 0.40 + 1.25 − 1 − 0.65 = 0 exactly.
candidates.suspected_defect: A strictly concave configuration satisfies C(r) = 0 for θ = π/2, so the claim that concave configurations are excluded from \tilde{C} is false. (More generally, for a concave configuration r13^2 = r14^2 + r23^2 − r24^2 + 2 r12 r34 cos(α+β), so C(r)=0 whenever cos θ = cos(α+β).) Moreover the same analysis shows \tilde{C} contains genuinely non-planar distance vectors, contrary to the implicit use of C=0 as a planarity-compatible constraint.

candidates.error_location: Proof of Lemma 2, list of eigenvalues ζ_1,…,ζ_4
candidates.claim_content: In the proof of Lemma 2 one has R_ij = m_i m_j (δ + 2/r_ij^3) with δ = λ/m > 0, S_ij = m_i m_j r_ij (δ − r_ij^{-3}), and the critical point equations (18) include S_13 − 2η r_13 = 0, S_14 + 2η r_14 = 0, S_23 + 2η r_23 = 0, S_24 − 2η r_24 = 0. From S_13 − 2η r_13 = 0 one gets 2η = S_13/r_13 = m_1 m_3 (δ − 1/r_13^3), so R_13 − 2η = m_1 m_3 (δ + 2/r_13^3 − δ + 1/r_13^3) = 3 m_1 m_3 / r_13^3, not m_1 m_3 / r_13^3. Similarly ζ_2 = R_14 + 2η = 3 m_1 m_4/r_14^3, ζ_3 = 3 m_2 m_3/r_23^3, ζ_4 = 3 m_2 m_4/r_24^3.
candidates.suspected_defect: The four stated eigenvalues are each off by a factor of 3 (they should be 3 m_i m_j / r_ij^3). Positivity, and hence the conclusion of Lemma 2, is unaffected, but the stated values are incorrect.

candidates.error_location: Proof of Lemma 2, expression for a_0 and its evaluation
candidates.claim_content: In the proof of Lemma 2, ζ_5 and ζ_6 are the two remaining eigenvalues of the 6x6 Hessian D^2 W(r), which are the eigenvalues of the 2x2 block [[R_12, 2η cos θ],[2η cos θ, R_34]] with R_ij = m_i m_j(δ + 2/r_ij^3). Therefore the product is a_0 = ζ_5 ζ_6 = det of that block = R_12 R_34 − 4 η^2 cos^2 θ. Using 2η cos θ = −S_12/r_34 = −S_34/r_12 with S_ij = m_i m_j r_ij (δ − r_ij^{-3}), one obtains a_0 = m_1m_2m_3m_4[(δ + 2/r_12^3)(δ + 2/r_34^3) − (δ − 1/r_12^3)(δ − 1/r_34^3)] = 3 m_1m_2m_3m_4 (1 + δ(r_12^3 + r_34^3))/(r_12^3 r_34^3). The paper instead writes a_0 = 4 r_12^3 r_13^6 r_14^6 r_23^6 r_24^6 r_34^3 ( R_12 R_34 − 4 η^2 r_12^3 r_34^3 cos^2 θ ) and concludes a_0 = 3 m_1m_2m_3m_4(1 + (r_12^3 + r_34^3) δ).
candidates.suspected_defect: The displayed formula for a_0 = ζ_5 ζ_6 contains a spurious prefactor 4 r_12^3 r_13^6 r_14^6 r_23^6 r_24^6 r_34^3 and a spurious factor r_12^3 r_34^3 multiplying 4η^2 cos^2 θ; the correct determinant of the 2x2 block is simply R_12 R_34 − 4 η^2 cos^2 θ. The stated final value also omits the factor 1/(r_12^3 r_34^3). Positivity (and hence Lemma 2) survives, but the formulas as written are wrong and mutually inconsistent.

candidates.error_location: Proof of Lemma 2, the two expressions for cos θ
candidates.claim_content: With S_12 = m_1 m_2 r_12 (δ − r_12^{-3}) and R_12 = m_1 m_2 (δ + 2/r_12^3), one has r_12 (R_12 − 3 m_1 m_2 / r_12^3) = m_1 m_2 r_12 (δ − 1/r_12^3) = S_12. Hence −S_12/(2η r_34) = − r_12 (R_12 − 3 m_1 m_2 / r_12^3)/(2 η r_34). The paper writes the right-hand side with a PLUS sign and with '3/r_12^3' instead of '3 m_1 m_2 / r_12^3'. The same two issues occur in the companion line cos θ = −S_34/(2η r_12) = r_34(R_34 − 3/r_34^3)/(2η r_12).
candidates.suspected_defect: Sign error (the identity gives −r_12(R_12 − 3m_1m_2/r_12^3)/(2ηr_34)) and a missing mass factor m_1 m_2 (resp. m_3 m_4). Because only cos^2 θ is subsequently used, the sign error does not propagate, but the equations as displayed are false.

candidates.error_location: Proof of Lemma 3, definition of D_1
candidates.exact_quote: then \(D_1\) is contractible in the 2-dimension \((r_{14}, r_{23})\)-plane, i.e., it forms a quarter of a disk with radius \(1/2\)
candidates.claim_content: D_1 is defined as D_1 = { (r_14, r_23) ∈ (R^+)^2 : 0 ≤ r_14^2 + r_23^2 = G_1 ≤ 1/2 }, i.e. the set of points of the closed first quadrant whose squared Euclidean norm is at most 1/2. Its radius is therefore sqrt(1/2) = 1/√2 ≈ 0.707, not 1/2.
candidates.suspected_defect: Stated radius 1/2 is incorrect; the quarter disk has radius 1/√2. (Contractibility, which is all that is used, is unaffected.)

candidates.error_location: Proof of Lemma 3, the fibration p : M_0^+ → D
candidates.exact_quote: For a fixed point \((r_{13}, r_{24}, r_{14}, r_{23}) \in D\), we find that \(v_1\) and \(w_1\) are determined uniquely by (22). Without loss of generality, we assume that \(w_1 = r_{12} - r_{34} \leq 0\) holds.
candidates.claim_content: In the proof of Lemma 3 one sets v_1 = r_12 + r_34 ≥ 0, w_1 = r_12 − r_34, G_1 = r_14^2 + r_23^2, G_2 = r_13^2 + r_24^2, Θ = 1/cos θ + 1, and the defining equations of M_0^+ become (22): v_1^2 + Θ G_1 = 1 + (Θ−2) G_2 and w_1^2 + Θ G_2 = 1 + (Θ−2) G_1. For fixed (r_13, r_24, r_14, r_23) these determine v_1^2 and w_1^2, hence v_1 = +sqrt(...) uniquely (since v_1 ≥ 0) but w_1 = ±sqrt(1 + (Θ−2)G_1 − Θ G_2), i.e. TWO values whenever that quantity is positive (corresponding to r_12 > r_34 and r_12 < r_34, which are genuinely different distance vectors since masses are not assumed symmetric). The paper asserts the fibre of p : M_0^+ → D is a single point and restricts to w_1 ≤ 0 'without loss of generality'.
candidates.suspected_defect: The fibre of the claimed fibration is generically two points, not one, so M_0^+ is a double of D glued along the locus w_1 = 0; the restriction w_1 ≤ 0 is not a 'without loss of generality' reduction for general (non-symmetric) masses. The Euler-characteristic conclusion χ(M^+)=1 may still hold (union of two contractible pieces along a contractible face), but the argument as written is incorrect/incomplete.

candidates.claim_content: In the proof of Proposition 2, after substituting r_13^2 = 2 r_12 r_34 cos θ + r_23^2 + r_14^2 − r_24^2 (Eq. (12)) into the Cayley–Menger determinant F_4(r), the paper asserts Eq. (13): F_4(r) = C(r)·A(r) − 2((A(r)/(4 r_24))^2 − B(r)^2), where C(r) = 2 r_12 r_34 cos θ + r_23^2 + r_14^2 − r_24^2 − r_13^2, A(r) is given by Eq. (14) and B(r) = sqrt(F_3(1,2,4) F_3(2,3,4))/(2 r_24) = 8 V_{124}V_{234}/r_24. Immediately afterwards the paper proves A(r) = 4 r_24 B(r), which makes the subtracted bracket identically zero, so (13) degenerates to (11). Also, substituting (12) into F_4 makes C(r) ≡ 0, so the first term of (13) vanishes identically and (13) reads 0 = −2((A/(4r_24))^2 − B^2).
candidates.suspected_defect: Equation (13) is internally inconsistent: under the substitution (12) the term C(r)·A(r) vanishes identically, and the bracket vanishes identically by the subsequently proved identity A = 4 r_24 B, so (13) carries no content and cannot be the stated decomposition of F_4 off the constraint set. It appears to confuse an identity valid only on {C=0} with one valid in a neighbourhood, which is exactly what Lemma 1's differentiation requires.

candidates.exact_quote: Here, we need to point out that $\eta \neq 0$ if and only if $r \in G$ is strictly convex or only $P_1, P_2$ and $P_3$ are collinear.
candidates.claim_content: In Proposition 3, η = σ · A(r) with A(r) = 32 V_{124} V_{234}, V_{ijk} the area of triangle P_iP_jP_k. Hence (given σ ≠ 0) η = 0 if and only if V_{124} = 0 or V_{234} = 0, i.e. if and only if P_1,P_2,P_4 are collinear or P_2,P_3,P_4 are collinear. The paper instead asserts η ≠ 0 iff the configuration is strictly convex or only P_1,P_2,P_3 are collinear.
candidates.suspected_defect: The stated characterisation does not match A(r) = 32 V_{124}V_{234}: η ≠ 0 also holds, e.g., when exactly P_1,P_3,P_4 are collinear, and the two degenerate cases that force η = 0 are the collinearity of {P_1,P_2,P_4} or {P_2,P_3,P_4}, not of {P_1,P_2,P_3}. Also σ ≠ 0 is tacitly assumed.

candidates.exact_quote: to replace all the mutual distances with \(d\) and sines, then we get \(C(r) - 2 \cos \theta P(r) = 0\). Since \(\cos \theta \not\equiv 0\), this implies that \(P(r) = 0\)
candidates.claim_content: In Remark 2 the authors consider a cyclic (co-circular) convex quadrilateral with circumdiameter d, use the law of sines r_12 = d sin ψ, r_13 = d sin(γ+α), r_14 = d sin α, r_23 = d sin β, r_24 = d sin(ψ+α), r_34 = d sin γ with (α+γ)+(β+ψ) = π, substitute into C(r) = 2 r_12 r_34 cos θ + r_23^2 + r_14^2 − r_24^2 − r_13^2 and conclude 'C(r) − 2 cos θ P(r) = 0', from which, since cos θ ≠ 0, they deduce P(r) = 0 (Ptolemy's relation). Note that on the co-circular family one already has C(r) = 0 (the quadrilateral is convex) and P(r) = 0 (Ptolemy's theorem), so the stated relation is 0 = 0 and the implication 'C − 2cosθ P = 0 and cos θ ≠ 0 ⟹ P = 0' only follows if C = 0 is known independently.
candidates.suspected_defect: The stated inference is a non sequitur as written: from an identity C − 2 cos θ P = 0 one gets P = 0 only after also knowing C = 0; moreover on the co-circular family both quantities vanish identically, so the derivation is circular and does not establish Ptolemy's theorem.

candidates.error_location: Proof of Lemma 3, final paragraph, definition of \mathcal{E}^5(1)
candidates.claim_content: The mutual-distance vector of four bodies is r = (r_12, r_13, r_14, r_23, r_24, r_34) ∈ R^6, and the quadratic form Σ_{i<j} m_i m_j r_ij^2 involves all six coordinates; the level set {Σ_{i<j} m_i m_j r_ij^2 = 1} is a 5-dimensional ellipsoid sitting inside R^6, not inside R^5. The paper writes r ∈ R^5 in the definition of E^5(1).
candidates.suspected_defect: Dimension mismatch in the definition: the ambient space must be R^6 (six mutual distances) for the sum over i<j ≤ 4 to make sense; as written the ellipsoid is defined over R^5.
